## Identification

The implementation in question is **`(*Command).Find`**, defined at **`command.go:755–779`** (this snapshot is module `github.com/spf13/cobra`, `go.mod:1`; no release tag is present in the files read, so the exact version is not determinable from evidence):

- Doc comment, `command.go:755–756`: “Find the target command given the args and command tree / Meant to be run on the highest node. Only searches down.”
- Signature, `command.go:757`: `func (c *Command) Find(args []string) (*Command, []string, error)`.

It is the non-`TraverseChildren` resolution path used by `ExecuteC`: `cmd, flags, err = c.Find(args)` at **`command.go:1123`**, inside the `if c.TraverseChildren { … } else { … }` split at `command.go:1120–1124`. The second return value (`flags`, i.e. the remaining arguments) is handed onward for later flag parsing/execution (`command.go:1137–1140` shows `cmd.commandCalledAs.called` being set right after the call, and the errors are reported at `command.go:1125–1135`), i.e. `Find` deliberately does not parse or consume flags itself.

## How it recurses and returns remaining arguments

Inside `Find` a closure `innerfind` is declared (`command.go:758–772`):

1. `argsWOflags := stripFlags(innerArgs, c)` (`:761`) — `stripFlags` (`command.go:674–710`) walks args, drops flags and flag values (handling `--flag value`, `-f value`, `=`-forms, `hasNoOptDefVal`/`shortHasNoOptDefVal`, and stopping at `--`), and returns only non-flag tokens.
2. If no such tokens remain, `return c, innerArgs` (`:762–764`) — the current command is the target and the *original inner args* (flags included) are returned.
3. Otherwise `nextSubCmd := argsWOflags[0]` (`:765`) and `cmd := c.findNext(nextSubCmd)` (`:767`).
4. On a match: `return innerfind(cmd, c.argsMinusFirstX(innerArgs, nextSubCmd))` (`:768–769`) — recursion descends into the child with the child-name token removed. `argsMinusFirstX` (`command.go:712–748`) removes only the **first** occurrence of that token while carefully skipping flag values (its comment notes the openshift `admin policy add-role-to-user admin` case), preserving all other args, including flags.
5. On no match: `return c, innerArgs` (`:770–771`) — the current command wins and the unconsumed args (flags and candidate positionals) are returned.

Then `Find` wraps the result (`:774–778`): if the found command has `Args == nil`, the error third value comes from `legacyArgs(commandFound, stripFlags(a, commandFound))`; otherwise the error is `nil`. `legacyArgs` (`args.go:24–39`) accepts anything when the command has no subcommands, but for a root command with subcommands and unconsumed args it returns `unknown command %q for %q%s` plus suggestions (`args.go:35–37`).

## Name and alias matching

`findNext` (`command.go:798–817`) iterates `c.commands` and accepts an exact-ish match when `commandNameMatches(cmd.Name(), next) || cmd.HasAlias(next)` (`:801`). `Name()` is the first word of `Use` (`command.go:1541–1548`); `HasAlias` (`command.go:1551–1558`) compares each entry of the command's `Aliases` with the same `commandNameMatches`. `commandNameMatches` (`command.go:1925–1934`) is `strings.EqualFold` when the global `EnableCaseInsensitive` is true, else plain `==`. On a match, `cmd.commandCalledAs.name = next` records the invoked spelling (`:802`) used by `CalledAs()` (`command.go:1562–1567`), and the command is returned immediately before any prefix logic.

## Prefix matching with multiple matches

Prefix matching is opt-in via the global `EnablePrefixMatching` (`cobra.go:46–55`: default `false`, comment warns it “can be a dangerous thing”). In `findNext`, unmatched-by-name children are collected only if `EnablePrefixMatching && cmd.hasNameOrAliasPrefix(next)` (`command.go:805–807`); `hasNameOrAliasPrefix` (`command.go:1571–1583`) tests `strings.HasPrefix` against `Name()` then each alias, and side-effects `commandCalledAs.name` to the matched name/alias.

Crucially, the exact-name/alias test precedes this and returns immediately, so prefix matching only applies to otherwise-unmatched tokens. If exactly one child matched, it is returned (`:810–813`); if **zero or more than one** matched, `findNext` returns `nil` (`:816`). Zero matches simply means “this arg isn't a child here.” For multiple matches, the nil is treated as no match at all: `innerfind` returns the parent plus the remaining args (`:770–771`), so no arbitrary branch is chosen. The token then survives as a positional argument of the parent — where, if the parent has subcommands and `Args == nil`, `legacyArgs` raises `unknown command` (`args.go:35–37`). The test table confirms this: with `EnablePrefixMatching=true` and sibling `child1`/`child2`, input `"th"` expects `call: ""` (“find/conflict”, `command_test.go:2484`), while `"thi"` resolves to `child1` via alias `this` (`command_test.go:2483`). Related tests: `TestEnablePrefixMatching` (`command_test.go:305–332`), `TestAliasPrefixMatching` (`command_test.go:334–367`), and `TestFind` (`command_test.go:2793–2880`), whose cases assert that flags interleaved with the child token (e.g. `{"-f","child","-b","something","child"}` → `{"-f","child","-b","something"}`, `command_test.go:2847–2848`) are retained in the returned args.

## Limitations

I did not execute code or tests; all behavior above is read from source and test expectations, and I did not read the code that consumes `Find`'s second return value past `command.go:1140` (dispatch budget exhausted), so the downstream flag-parsing step is inferred from the call site. The snapshot carries no version tag in the files inspected.
